title: CP53E Notices Are Back After October 15: Check Every Client's 2025 Overpayment Election Against the Transcript and the Bank Feed, and Rebuild the January 15 Estimate Before the Penalty Clock Runs
excerpt: A new round of CP53E notices went out after October 15 to clients who elected to apply 2025 overpayments to 2026 estimated tax, and the AICPA says the IRS has not explained why. If the IRS refunded the money instead of crediting it, the April installment was never paid and the underpayment penalty is running. Here is the transcript check, the bank feed match, the equity entry for a refund that hit the business account, and the pay-now versus December-withholding decision to make before January 15.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: CPA firm worksheet for a CP53E notice review showing each client's 2025 overpayment election, the transcript result of credited or refunded, the bank feed match, and the rebuilt January 15 estimate with the pay-now or withholding remedy
content:
A CP53E notice after October 15 means the IRS may have refunded a 2025 overpayment your client elected to apply to 2026 estimated tax. Before January 15, pull each affected client's account transcript, match any refund to the bank feed, rebuild the estimate, and decide whether to pay now or raise December withholding.

Why the CP53E notice is back on the CPA's desk now

The Journal of Accountancy reported on a new round of CP53E notices, published 2026-11-23, involving 2025 overpayments that clients elected to apply to their 2026 tax. The notices went out after the October 15 extended filing deadline. At an AICPA Town Hall on November 12, Daniel Hauffe, the AICPA's senior manager for Tax Policy and Advocacy, said the AICPA had asked the IRS whether the notices were issued in error, and as of the following week 'the AICPA had not received a response from the IRS.' The accounting problem is stated in one sentence from the article: 'If these overpayments are refunded rather than credited, then 2026 estimated payments are thrown off, leading to underpayment penalties.' Earlier notices had been traced to IRS adjustments that increased the refund beyond the amount carried forward. The article says the new ones reportedly do not involve such adjustments.

The IRS page Understanding your CP53E notice, last updated 2026-05-11, explains when the notice is issued: 'Your tax return shows a refund, but the bank information is invalid, missing, or rejected, or a return with a balance due is corrected by the IRS and now results in a refund.' The taxpayer has 30 days to add a bank account through an IRS Online Account, the update can't be made by phone, there is one opportunity to add or update the account, and if there is no response the IRS issues a paper check after six weeks. The notice exists because of Executive Order 14247, signed March 25, 2025, which the IRS describes on its payments modernization page, updated 2026-09-25: paper refund checks are being phased out, starting with individual taxpayers, because 'paper checks are over 16 times more likely to be lost, stolen, altered, or delayed than electronic payments.'

This is the third round of the same problem in one year. On 2026-05-08 The Tax Adviser reported more than 1.4 million CP53E notices and an IRS acknowledgment that some went to taxpayers whose overpayments were scheduled to be applied to 2026 estimated tax, with the IRS saying that 'until further guidance is issued, the IRS is not recommending any further action.' On June 9 the AICPA sent the IRS a letter asking it to clarify the reasons a CP53E notice would be issued, define every category of excepted taxpayer, let taxpayers self-identify on the return, and stop sending the notice to people who had already been excepted. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration's report The IRS's Paperless Transition Efforts as of July 2026, issued 2026-09-14, put the count at 4.2 million individual taxpayers, with 300,537 exceptions granted by March 30, and concluded, as the Journal of Accountancy summarized on 2026-09-18, that 'more public outreach to stakeholders and taxpayers could have increased awareness of the EO and reduced confusion with the notice.' Then on 2026-11-16 the IRS opened its Get Ready series with IR-2026-140, repeating that it is phasing out paper refund checks starting with individuals. The fourth 2026 installment is due January 15, 2027, which the IRS estimated tax schedule, updated 2026-10-02, states as 'Jan. 15 of the following year.' That is the deadline this review works toward.

Coverage outside the profession's own press explains what the notice is. A CPA firm's explainer from 2026-07-21 covers why the notice confuses people, notes that some went out in error when an overpayment was applied to 2026 estimates, and tells readers to check their Online Account and call the office. It doesn't cover the underpayment penalty, how to rebuild the estimate, or how to prove from the transcript and the bank feed what the IRS actually did. That is what this article covers.

What an applied overpayment is, and what changes when the IRS refunds it

On the 2025 Form 1040, line 34 is the overpayment, line 35a is the part refunded, and line 36 is the part applied to 2026 estimated tax. The two parts add to line 34. The Form 1040 instructions say the election to apply the overpayment to the next year can't be changed later, and the IRS treats the credited amount as paid toward the first 2026 installment, which was due April 15, 2026. For a CPA, line 36 is a payment that was never made in cash. It sits in the firm's estimate schedule as the April installment and nowhere else.

That is why a refund of that amount is an accounting event and not just a notice. The required annual payment, per IRS Tax Topic 306, updated 2026-09-24, is met when a taxpayer has 'paid withholding and estimated tax of at least 90% of the tax for the current year or 100% of the tax shown on the return for the prior year, whichever is smaller,' and Form 1040-ES substitutes 110 percent for 100 percent when prior-year adjusted gross income was above $150,000. The payment is tested installment by installment on Form 2210. Remove the April installment and every later quarter is short by the same amount, with the penalty running from April 15 until the shortfall is covered. Two rules decide the fix. An estimated payment counts on the date it is paid. Withholding is treated as paid in equal parts on each of the four due dates unless the taxpayer shows when it was actually withheld, so withholding added in December reaches back to April.

The books matter for a different reason. A refund that lands in a pass-through owner's business checking account, which happens when the return listed that account, is not income. It is the owner's personal money arriving in the entity: debit cash, credit owner's equity as a contribution. The entity never carried the owner's income tax, so there is no tax expense to reduce. When the client later pays the replacement estimate from the business account, that is a draw: debit owner's equity, credit cash. For a C corporation client, the credited overpayment is a prepaid income tax asset at a point in time, and a refund is debit cash, credit prepaid tax, with the estimate to be paid again. Book it as income or expense and the profit and loss is wrong for the year while the balance sheet quietly carries the error.

One firm, 310 individual clients, one week: the walk-through

Call the firm Larkspur Tax and Advisory: 310 individual returns, 140 of them Schedule C owners, partners, or S corporation shareholders whose books the firm also keeps in QuickBooks Online. Two CPAs, three preparers, one admin. The figures are illustrative; the sequence is the point.

Step one: build the election register from the 2025 returns

The admin exports every 2025 return with a nonzero line 36. There are 96, applying a total of $1,418,500 to 2026. Each row carries the client, entity type, amount applied, 2025 total tax, 2025 adjusted gross income for the 110 percent test, the 2026 installments paid so far by quarter and date, the bank account listed on the return, and whether the client has reported a CP53E notice. Eleven have. The register takes about two hours and is the document everything else ties to.

Step two: pull the transcript for all 96, not just the 11

A notice can be lost in the mail or sitting in a client's inbox. The firm pulls the 2025 account transcript for every client on the register through its practitioner access, the same channel it set up when it built its Tax Pro Account payment register. At about four minutes per transcript the pull takes a preparer most of a day. The result: 88 transcripts show the credit elect transferred to 2026 with no refund. Eight show a refund issued. Five of the eight had reported a notice; three had not. Six clients who reported a notice show an intact credit, which matches the AICPA's suspicion that the new round includes notices issued in error. Their transcripts go in the file and their bank feeds go on a six-week watch list.

Step three: match every refund to a bank feed

The eight refunds total $212,400. The firm searches the bank feeds it holds for IRS Treasury deposits and for check deposits matching each refund amount after October 15. Three refunds landed in business checking accounts, because those owners listed the business account on the return. One of them, $31,200 for a Schedule C client, had been booked by the client's in-house bookkeeper to Other Income. The preparer reclassifies it to owner contribution, which takes $31,200 out of the year's profit and puts it in equity where it belongs. Two refunds show no deposit anywhere; those clients never added a bank account within the 30 days, so a paper check is expected about six weeks after the window closed, and the register records the expected amount. Three landed in personal accounts.

Step four: rebuild the 2026 estimate for the eight

Take one of them. Marisol Quint, a Schedule C consultant, showed $48,000 of 2025 tax on adjusted gross income of $210,000, so her required annual payment is 110 percent of $48,000, or $52,800, in four installments of $13,200. She applied $14,000 from 2025 to cover April and paid $13,200 in June and September. Her transcript shows the $14,000 refunded in late October to her personal account. The schedule now reads April unpaid, and the cumulative shortfall is $13,200 at each of the three due dates so far. Her options, which the CPA lays out side by side: pay $14,000 now through an electronic method the firm can reconcile to the confirmation, which stops the penalty on the April shortfall from the payment date; or have her spouse raise December W-2 withholding by $14,000, which Form 2210 spreads as $3,500 to each due date and cuts the April shortfall to $9,700, June to $6,200, and September to $2,700; or do both. In every case the January 15 installment of $13,200 is still due. The CPA records the choice, the amounts, and the dates on the register.

Step five: fix the 2026 return before it is prepared

Tax software carries the prior-year applied amount forward into the current-year payments automatically. For the eight refunded clients, the firm overrides that carryforward now, while the register is open, so the 2026 return claims only payments the IRS actually holds. A return that claims a $14,000 payment the IRS refunded will mismatch and generate another notice in 2027. The firm also writes to all 96 clients: the notice gives one 30-day chance to add a bank account online, the IRS won't take bank details by phone, and the 2026 return should carry a valid direct deposit account so the next refund never triggers a CP53E notice at all. For a firm that also provides outsourced accounting services, the register becomes part of the year-end close file for every pass-through client.

The time: about two hours on the register, six and a half on transcripts, an hour and a half on bank feeds, four hours on the eight rebuilds, and an hour on client letters, roughly 15 hours across the firm. The alternative was finding out in March 2027, when the first mismatch notice arrives, that an estimate the client thought was paid in April never existed.

Accounting controls for the CP53E notice review

Source data: the 2025 returns as filed, with lines 34, 35a, and 36 and the bank account on the return; the 2025 account transcript for every client with a nonzero line 36, pulled after the notice date; the CP53E notices clients forwarded, with their dates; any IRS adjustment notice for the same year; the bank feeds for business accounts the firm holds and the client's confirmation for personal accounts; the 2026 installments paid, with confirmation numbers and dates; and the dated IRS and AICPA pages the firm relied on, including the CP53E page updated 2026-05-11 and the Journal of Accountancy report of 2026-11-23.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Line 35a plus line 36 equals line 34 on every return in the register. For each client, the required annual payment is the smaller of 90 percent of projected 2026 tax or 100 percent of 2025 tax, 110 percent when 2025 adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000, divided into four installments. Cumulative payments at each due date equal the applied overpayment, if the transcript shows it intact, plus estimated payments on the dates paid, plus withholding spread equally across the four dates. The shortfall at each due date is the cumulative requirement minus cumulative payments, floored at zero. For a refund found in a business account, the entry is debit cash, credit owner's equity for a pass-through, or debit cash, credit prepaid income tax for a C corporation, and the amount equals the transcript's refund to the cent. A replacement estimate paid from the business account is debit owner's equity, credit cash.

Review: a second preparer, not the one who built the register, confirms that every client with a nonzero line 36 has a transcript on file, that each transcript's outcome is coded to one of the four rows in the table above, that every refund issued has been matched to a deposit or to an expected paper check, that every refund in a business account was reclassified out of income or expense, that the carryforward override is set for every refunded client, and that each rebuilt schedule shows the chosen remedy with dates. Any transcript the firm can't pull is an open item, not a presumed credit.

Decision: the signing CPA owns the remedy for each refunded client, pay now, add withholding, or both, and documents why. The client owns the choice to add a bank account within the 30-day window and the direct deposit account on the 2026 return. The preparer owns the register and the override. The firm's tax lead decides whether to send the AICPA examples of notices that appear to have been issued in error, since that is what the AICPA is collecting for the IRS.

Limits and common mistakes

The IRS has not said why the post-October notices were issued, and the AICPA's question was unanswered when this was written. Nothing here presumes the notices are wrong or right. The transcript decides, client by client.

Don't treat a CP53E notice as proof of a refund, and don't treat the absence of one as proof of a credit. Three of the eight refunds in the walk-through reached clients who never reported a notice.

Don't let an IRS refund sit in Other Income or reduce an expense line. For a pass-through owner it is equity. For a C corporation it is the reversal of a prepaid asset.

Don't rebuild the estimate on the current-year projection alone when the prior-year safe harbor is lower. Test both, and apply 110 percent when 2025 adjusted gross income was above $150,000.

Don't assume December withholding cures the whole year. It is spread equally across the four due dates, so it reduces each earlier shortfall by a quarter of the added amount. A cash payment stops the clock only from the day it is paid.

Don't leave the software's carryforward in place for a refunded client. The 2026 return will claim a payment the IRS doesn't hold.

Larkspur Tax and Advisory, Marisol Quint, and their figures are illustrative. The notice behavior, windows, and dates come from the IRS, TIGTA, and AICPA sources cited above. Penalty rates change quarterly and are not stated here; Form 2210 and its instructions govern the computation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a CP53E notice mean when the client applied the overpayment to 2026 estimated tax?

The IRS sends a CP53E notice when a return shows a refund but the bank information is missing, invalid, or rejected, or when the IRS corrects a return and a refund results. If the client elected on line 36 of the 2025 Form 1040 to apply the overpayment to 2026, the notice may have been issued in error, as the IRS acknowledged in May 2026, or the IRS may have refunded the amount. Only the account transcript shows which happened.

How do I tell whether the IRS credited or refunded the overpayment?

Pull the client's 2025 account transcript. A credit elect transferred to the next period with no refund transaction means the election held. A refund issued transaction means the money went out by direct deposit or, if nobody added a bank account within 30 days, by paper check about six weeks later. Match any refund to the client's bank feed by amount and date.

What happens to the 2026 estimated tax if the overpayment was refunded?

The credited amount was meant to cover the first 2026 installment due April 15, 2026. If it was refunded, that installment is unpaid from that date, and the underpayment penalty on Form 2210 runs until the shortfall is covered. Paying the amount now stops the clock from the payment date. Extra withholding before December 31 is treated as paid evenly across the four due dates, which reduces the earlier shortfalls.

Should the client respond to the CP53E notice if the overpayment was correctly credited?

In May 2026 the IRS said it was not recommending any further action until it issued more guidance, and the AICPA is asking whether the new round of notices after October 15 was also issued in error. The firm should document the transcript showing the credit elect, watch the bank feed for an unexpected refund, and tell the client that the notice gives one 30-day chance to add a bank account online.

How should a refund that lands in a business bank account be booked?

For a sole proprietor, partner, or S corporation shareholder, a personal tax refund deposited to the business account is an owner contribution: debit cash, credit owner's equity. It is not income, and it is not a reduction of tax expense, because a pass-through entity does not carry the owner's income tax. If the client later pays the estimate from the business account, record it as a draw.

Once every client's election, transcript result, deposit, and remedy sit in one register, the firm can see which pass-through clients have an IRS deposit booked to income, which still have an open paper check, and which schedules were rebuilt, across all 96 files, before the January 15 installment rather than after the first mismatch notice.
